exercise1.prompt: Selecting What You Need: Tidy the column names

hiddenCases.name: already tidy names are left alone

exercise1.hint: Build a dictionary from each existing name to its tidy version, then hand it to rename. str.lower() and str.replace(" ", "_") do the work.

exercise2.prompt: Selecting What You Need: Read only what you need

hiddenCases.name: one column is a valid request
the rows are unaffected by the column choice

exercise2.hint: pd.read_csv(path, usecols=keep) then .shape. Reading everything and then selecting gives the same shape but does all the work you were trying to avoid.

choices: Reads only the columns you name
questions.explain: Less memory, and fewer unchecked columns to surprise you later.

questions.prompt: How do you rename several columns at once?
choices: Both of the first two work
questions.explain: Assigning to df.columns replaces all of them positionally; rename maps the ones you name and leaves the rest.

questions.prompt: An id column of 007 read normally becomes what?
questions.explain: It is read as a number, and numbers have no leading zeros. dtype={"id": str} keeps it as text.

questions.prompt: Why does an id read as a number in one file and text in another matter?
choices: A later join will match nothing, and will not raise
questions.explain: 3 and "3" are different keys. The merge succeeds with an empty result, which is the quietest failure in unit 8.
